knowledge_meta.name: Manufacturing Operations
knowledge_meta.description: Discrete and process manufacturing. Covers production tracking, quality control, inventory management, COGS lineage, and month-end close.

phases.name: Business Questions
phases.description: Identify the top financial questions leadership asks about manufacturing performance

questions.text: What are the top 3 financial questions your leadership asks each period about manufacturing performance?
follow_ups: How quickly do you need these answers — real-time, daily, or month-end?
Do you need answers at the plant level, product level, or both?
hints: Common: 'What's our COGS?', 'What's our yield/scrap rate?', 'Are we hitting production targets?', 'What's the variance to standard cost?'
COGS (Cost of Goods Sold) is typically the #1 financial question in manufacturing
Standard cost vs actual cost variance is a key control metric

questions.text: How do you calculate Cost of Goods Sold? What components go into it?
follow_ups: Is it standard costing or actual costing?
How do you handle overhead allocation?
hints: COGS = Material Cost + Labor Cost + Overhead. Each has sub-components
Material: raw material consumption, BOM (Bill of Materials) costing, purchase price variance
Labor: direct labor hours × rate, shift premiums, overtime
Overhead: machine hours × rate, utilities, depreciation — allocated per cost center or product
Standard costing: compare actual to standard, analyse variances (price, usage, efficiency)

questions.text: Walk me through your month-end close for manufacturing. What's the sequence and what takes the longest?
follow_ups: How many days after month-end do you have final numbers?
What's the biggest bottleneck?
hints: Typical sequence: production cutoff → inventory count/valuation → goods issue posting → labor posting → overhead allocation → variance analysis → GL close
Production cutoff (confirming all production orders) is often the bottleneck
Inventory valuation depends on completed production orders — delays cascade
WIP (Work in Progress) valuation is particularly tricky — partly completed orders

questions.text: How do you track inventory value? Is it real-time or do you rely on periodic physical counts?
follow_ups: How often do you do physical inventory counts?
What's the typical variance between system and physical count?
hints: Perpetual inventory (real-time system tracking) vs periodic (physical count-based)
Even with perpetual systems, physical counts reveal discrepancies — cycle counting vs full count
Inventory accuracy directly affects COGS accuracy
WMS (Warehouse Management System) data vs ERP inventory records — reconciliation needed

common_metrics.name: Cost of Goods Sold (COGS)
common_metrics.business_question: What does it cost us to produce what we sell?

common_metrics.name: Inventory Valuation
common_metrics.business_question: What's our inventory worth and is it accurate?

common_metrics.name: Cost Variance Analysis
common_metrics.business_question: Why do our actual costs differ from standard?

questions.text: Let's define your COGS precisely. Which cost elements are included, and at what level do you track them?
follow_ups: Do you use standard cost or actual cost for reporting?
How are standard costs set and how often are they updated?
hints: Direct material: raw material per BOM × purchase price (or standard price)
Direct labor: hours × labor rate by cost center
Variable overhead: machine hours × variable rate
Fixed overhead: allocated based on volume or activity

phases.name: Measure Tracing
phases.description: Trace manufacturing financial metrics to their source data

questions.text: For material cost, where does the consumption data come from? Is it based on actual consumption or BOM-based backflushing?
follow_ups: How accurate is the BOM — is it maintained?
What happens with scrap and rework — is it captured?
hints: Backflushing: system calculates material based on BOM × production quantity. Simple but inaccurate if BOM is wrong or scrap isn't captured
Actual consumption: operators record what they actually used. More accurate but requires discipline
Scrap/rework creates a gap between BOM consumption and actual consumption

phases.name: Data Sourcing
phases.description: Identify system sources for manufacturing financial data

questions.text: Which systems hold the production data that feeds your financial reports? Is it one ERP or multiple systems?
follow_ups: Is there a gap between what the shop floor system records and what the ERP sees?
How is data transferred between systems — real-time integration or batch?
hints: Common pattern: MES (shop floor) → ERP (financial posting). Integration quality varies
Real-time integration means financial data is current. Batch (daily/weekly) means lag
Manual bridges (Excel uploads) between systems are a data quality risk
Look for: shop floor systems, WMS, quality systems, ERP, costing systems

typical_systems.name: ERP
typical_systems.role: Financial system of record — production orders, material management, costing, GL

typical_systems.name: MES (Manufacturing Execution System)
typical_systems.role: Shop floor execution — production confirmations, quality data, machine data

typical_systems.name: WMS (Warehouse Management System)
typical_systems.role: Inventory tracking — goods receipt, storage, picking, shipping

phases.name: Monitoring & KPIs
phases.description: Understand how production managers monitor performance

questions.text: What do you check first thing at the start of a shift or day to know if production is on track?
follow_ups: Is this data on a dashboard, a whiteboard, or in your head?
How quickly do you know when something goes wrong?
hints: Common: OEE, production output vs plan, downtime, quality rejects, safety incidents
Real-time visibility vs end-of-shift reports — the gap determines response time
Whiteboard/paper-based tracking = manual data entry opportunity

questions.text: How do you measure production efficiency? Do you use OEE or a different approach?
follow_ups: What are your current OEE targets?
Which of the three OEE components (availability, performance, quality) is the biggest challenge?
hints: OEE = Availability × Performance × Quality. World-class = 85%+
Availability: uptime / planned production time. Affected by breakdowns, changeovers, setup
Performance: actual output / theoretical max output. Affected by slow cycles, minor stops
Quality: good parts / total parts. Affected by defects, rework, scrap

common_metrics.name: OEE (Overall Equipment Effectiveness)
common_metrics.business_question: How effectively are we using our equipment?

common_metrics.name: Production Output vs Plan
common_metrics.business_question: Are we producing what we planned to produce?

common_metrics.name: Quality Performance
common_metrics.business_question: What's our defect/scrap rate and is it improving?

common_metrics.name: On-Time Delivery
common_metrics.business_question: Are we delivering to customers on time?

phases.name: Connect Up to Financial
phases.description: Link production KPIs to financial impact

questions.text: How does production performance affect your costs? For example, what's the cost of scrap or downtime?
follow_ups: Can you put a £/$ value on 1% improvement in OEE?
Are these cost impacts tracked or estimated?
hints: Scrap cost = scrap quantity × material cost. Often surprisingly large
Downtime cost = lost production minutes × production rate × margin per unit
Quality failures: internal (scrap/rework cost) + external (returns, warranty, reputation)

phases.name: Connect Down to Operational
phases.description: Link management monitoring to shop floor data

questions.text: What data do you need from the shop floor that you don't currently get reliably?
follow_ups: Is the data captured but not surfaced? Or not captured at all?
What would change if you had perfect real-time visibility?
hints: Common gaps: actual cycle times, root cause of downtime, operator-level quality data
Data captured on paper but not digitised is a common pattern in manufacturing
Real-time visibility enables proactive intervention vs reactive firefighting

phases.name: Pain Points
phases.description: Identify management pain points in manufacturing

questions.text: What's the most manual or time-consuming part of your production management process?
follow_ups: How many hours per week does this take?
Are there any whiteboards or paper logs that should be digital?
hints: Production scheduling done in Excel instead of planning system
Quality data captured on paper inspection sheets
Shift handover done verbally without documentation
Downtime logging done retrospectively at end of shift

phases.name: Systems & People
phases.description: Map the shop floor systems and roles

questions.text: Walk me through a typical production shift. What happens from start to finish, and what systems are involved?
follow_ups: At which points do operators interact with systems (scan, enter, confirm)?
Are there any steps that are still paper-based?
hints: Typical flow: receive work order → stage materials → set up machine → run production → confirm quantities → quality check → goods receipt
Each system interaction is a data capture point. Each paper step is a data gap
Look for: MES terminals, barcode scanners, quality stations, ERP confirmations

questions.text: Who are the key roles on the shop floor? Who creates data vs who consumes reports?
follow_ups: Which roles bridge between shop floor and office/management?
Are there any roles that do significant data entry as part of their job?
hints: Common roles: Machine Operator, Quality Inspector, Shift Supervisor, Material Handler, Maintenance Technician, Production Planner
Shift Supervisors often bridge shop floor and management — they're the key data producers
Quality Inspectors produce critical data (pass/fail, measurements) that feeds metrics

phases.name: Data Creation
phases.description: Understand where production data is born

questions.text: When a production order is completed, what exactly gets recorded and in which system?
follow_ups: Is the confirmation automatic (machine data) or manual (operator enters)?
What's the typical delay between completing production and confirming in the system?
hints: Production confirmation typically records: quantity produced, quantity scrapped, labor time, machine time
Automatic confirmation from MES = high accuracy. Manual SAP confirmation at end of shift = lower accuracy
The delay between production and confirmation directly affects financial data freshness
Backflushing materials vs actual consumption recording — a key design choice

questions.text: How is quality data captured? Is there an inspection system, or is it done on paper/Excel?
follow_ups: Is quality checked at every stage or only at final inspection?
How is non-conformance handled — is there a formal NCR process?
hints: In-process inspection vs end-of-line inspection — affects when quality problems are caught
SPC (Statistical Process Control) data from machines = real-time quality monitoring
Paper inspection sheets = data exists but isn't digitised or analysable
NCR (Non-Conformance Report) process tracks defects but often lags behind production

questions.text: What are the main things you work with — production orders, work orders, batches, lots? What's the hierarchy?
follow_ups: Can you trace a finished product back to its raw materials?
How do you track material lots for quality traceability?
hints: Common hierarchy: Sales Order → Production Order → Operation/Routing Step → Material Component
Lot/batch traceability is critical in regulated industries (pharma, food)
Bill of Materials (BOM) defines the material structure; Routing defines the process steps
Work center / machine is the physical resource where production happens

questions.text: What's the most frustrating part of the production process from a data/systems perspective?
follow_ups: Are there any paper-based workarounds that everyone relies on?
What data would you love to have that you don't currently get?
hints: Common frustrations: slow ERP confirmations, duplicate data entry, poor quality data integration
Paper travelers that carry production information between stations
Manual downtime logging that's often incomplete or inaccurate
Inventory discrepancies discovered during physical counts

cross_perspective_connections.description: COGS requires production confirmations, material consumption, and labor recording from the shop floor

cross_perspective_connections.description: Cost variances require management's production planning data to calculate efficiency and volume variances
cross_perspective_connections.suggested_question: How are standard costs set and maintained? Who owns the variance analysis?

cross_perspective_connections.description: Production KPIs depend on accurate shop floor data capture
cross_perspective_connections.suggested_question: How is downtime/scrap data captured on the shop floor — automatically or manually?

cross_perspective_connections.trigger_when: cost of downtime|cost of scrap|cost of quality
cross_perspective_connections.description: Production inefficiency needs financial quantification to justify improvement investment
cross_perspective_connections.suggested_question: Can you put a financial value on this production issue? What does 1% improvement save?

cross_perspective_connections.description: Untracked operational data means missing management visibility
cross_perspective_connections.suggested_question: Is anyone monitoring this data at a management level? What decisions would it inform?

cross_perspective_connections.description: Inventory movements drive financial valuations and COGS
cross_perspective_connections.suggested_question: How do inventory transactions become financial entries? Is it real-time or batch?

core_entities.name: Production Order
core_entities.description: An instruction to produce a quantity of a product

perspective_lenses.operational: A work instruction — what to produce, how much, on which machine, with what materials
perspective_lenses.management: A performance unit — on time, on quality, on cost. Completion tracking
perspective_lenses.financial: A cost collector — all material, labor, and overhead costs accumulated against this order

core_entities.name: Material / Product
core_entities.description: A raw material, semi-finished good, or finished product

perspective_lenses.operational: Something we consume, transform, or produce. What's in stock? What's needed?
perspective_lenses.management: A unit of analysis — yield rates, quality metrics, demand forecasting
perspective_lenses.financial: A cost carrier — standard cost, actual cost, purchase price, valuation

core_entities.name: Work Center / Machine
core_entities.description: A physical location or machine where production operations are performed

perspective_lenses.operational: Where I work — what's running, what's broken, what needs maintenance
perspective_lenses.management: A capacity unit — OEE, utilisation, planned vs actual hours
perspective_lenses.financial: A cost center — overhead rates, depreciation, maintenance costs

core_entities.name: Quality Inspection
core_entities.description: A quality check performed on materials or production output

perspective_lenses.operational: A check I perform — pass/fail, measurements, visual inspection
perspective_lenses.management: Quality performance data — first pass yield, defect patterns, SPC
perspective_lenses.financial: Cost of quality — scrap value, rework cost, warranty exposure

core_entities.name: Inventory Location
core_entities.description: A physical or logical storage location for materials

perspective_lenses.operational: Where things are — put away, pick, move, count
perspective_lenses.management: Accuracy and flow — inventory turns, fill rates, space utilisation
perspective_lenses.financial: Valuation — stock value, ageing, write-downs, carrying cost

terms.BOM: Bill of Materials — list of raw materials and components needed to produce a product
terms.Routing: Sequence of operations (steps) required to produce a product, with time and resource requirements
terms.OEE: Overall Equipment Effectiveness — Availability × Performance × Quality
terms.COGS: Cost of Goods Sold — total production cost of goods sold in a period
terms.WIP: Work in Progress — partially completed production orders, valued at accumulated costs
terms.Backflushing: Automatic material consumption posting based on BOM when production is confirmed
terms.Goods Issue: Material movement from warehouse to production — reduces inventory, increases WIP
terms.Goods Receipt: Material movement from production to warehouse — reduces WIP, increases finished goods inventory
terms.Standard Cost: Predetermined cost per unit used for planning and variance analysis
terms.Variance: Difference between standard (planned) and actual cost — analysed by type (price, usage, efficiency, volume)
terms.Cycle Time: Time to produce one unit — theoretical vs actual
terms.Changeover: Time to switch a machine from one product to another — a key OEE loss
terms.Scrap: Material that cannot be used or sold — waste from production process
terms.Rework: Product that doesn't meet quality standards but can be corrected — adds cost
terms.NCR: Non-Conformance Report — formal documentation of a quality failure
terms.SPC: Statistical Process Control — using statistical methods to monitor and control production quality
terms.MES: Manufacturing Execution System — shop floor system for real-time production tracking
terms.WMS: Warehouse Management System — system for inventory storage and movement tracking
terms.Lot/Batch: A quantity of material produced together, tracked for traceability
terms.Crystallisation: The moment when operational data becomes a frozen fact — e.g., production cutoff crystallises quantities for financial reporting
